Empirical Research Plan: “Trade-Policy Uncertainty, China’s WTO Accession, and U.S. Import Outcomes”

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
• Method: Difference-in-Differences with Continuous-Intensity Treatment, embedded in a Triple-Difference (DDD) framework and estimated in an event-study specification.  

• Rationale  
  – The “experiment’’ is the December-2001 granting of Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) to China, which eliminated the possibility that U.S. tariffs on Chinese goods would jump from the MFN rate to the much higher Column-2 rate.  
  – The ex-ante tariff gap gᵢ  =  Column2ᵢ  –  MFNᵢ, measured at the HS-6 industry level, captures how much policy uncertainty was removed. The gap is predetermined (set under the 1930 tariff schedule and 1980s MFN liberalisations) and does not change at the event date, so it is plausibly exogenous to China’s contemporary export performance.  
  – A simple U.S.-only DID (high-gap vs. low-gap industries, pre vs. post) might be confounded by China-specific supply shocks or global demand shocks that happen to differ by industry. Adding comparison destinations (EU, Japan) that did not change policy toward China at that moment implements a DDD and tightens the counterfactual trend.  
  – Annual data 1996-2006 allow an event-study to examine pre-trends and dynamic effects.  

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
  TREATᵢ = (gᵢ − g̃) / 100  or a high-gap indicator 1[gᵢ > median]. (I will use the continuous gap in the main specification and binary in robustness checks.)

Control group(s)  
  • Within the United States: industries with low or zero gaps provide within-country control.  
  • Across destinations: Chinese exports to the EU15 and Japan serve as external controls because their tariff-uncertainty regime did not change in 2001.

Treatment timing  
  Postₜ = 1 for t ≥ 2002 (calendar year after PNTR became effective); 0 for 1996-2001.

DDD regression structure
  ln X​ᵢdₜ  = α + β (Postₜ × US_d × TREATᵢ) + γ₁(Postₜ × US_d) + γ₂(US_d × TREATᵢ)  
              + γ₃(Postₜ × TREATᵢ) + δᵢ + δ_dₜ + ε​ᵢdₜ  

  where i = HS-6 industry, d ∈ {US, EU, JP}, t = year, δᵢ = industry FE, δ_dₜ = destination-year FE.

The coefficient of interest β is the causal effect of eliminating trade-policy uncertainty per 1-percentage-point of the threat gap.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends (conditional)  
  – In the absence of PNTR, the differential evolution of high-gap vs. low-gap products exported to the U.S. would have matched that in the EU/Japan.  
  – Plausibility: EU and Japan experienced similar macro shocks and Chinese supply expansions but did not alter policy uncertainty, making them credible controls. Pre-trend tests will be performed with the event-study.

A2. Exogeneity of the gap  
  – The Column-2 schedule is a 1930 artifact; MFN rates changed little around 2001. Hence gᵢ is predetermined relative to export growth during 1996-2006.

A3. No other contemporaneous U.S. policy changed differentially by gᵢ  
  – The MFA phase-out (mostly textile/apparel) and anti-dumping actions might violate this. We will control for industry-specific MFA quota fill rates and AD/CVD or safeguard dummies.

A4. Stable unit treatment value (SUTVA)  
  – An industry’s treatment should not affect other industries’ export growth through re-classification or direct spillovers. Given HS-6 fixed definitions, this seems reasonable, but we will inspect re-definitions.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. MFA quota abolition coincides with PNTR for textiles/apparel (high gaps).  
  – Mitigation: (i) add product-year MFA quota indicators or interaction terms; (ii) estimate results excluding HS-6 codes covered by the MFA and show that β remains.

T2. Endogenous anti-dumping / safeguard petitions post-PNTR, possibly targeted toward high-gap sectors.  
  – Mitigation: control for AD/CVD and safeguard dummies interacted with Post; run robustness dropping HS-6 × year observations under such measures.

T3. Industry re-classification or data quality changes around 2002.  
  – Mitigation: use concordances to create consistent HS-6 definitions over time; collapse to HS-4 as robustness; check for mass entry/exit of codes.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# -------------- 0. Packages -----------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # regressions with high-dimensional FE
library(ggplot2)      # event-study plots

# -------------- 1. Load Data ----------------
# Assume three csv files: trade.csv, tariffs.csv, policy_controls.csv
trade   <- fread("trade_panel_1996_2006.csv")          # HS6 × dest × year
tariffs <- fread("tariff_gaps.csv")                    # HS6 × gap
policy  <- fread("policy_controls.csv")                # HS6 × year × controls

# -------------- 2. Merge & Construct --------
df <- merge(trade, tariffs, by = "hs6")
df <- merge(df, policy,  by = c("hs6","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# Destination flag
df[, us := as.integer(dest == "US")]

# Treatment: continuous gap (in pct points)
df[, treat := gap]                     # e.g., 25.3 means 25.3 pct-pts
df[, post  := as.integer(year >= 2002)]

# Main interaction
df[, int_post_us_treat := post * us * treat]

# Log exports (+1 to keep zeros)
df[, ln_exports := log(export_value + 1)]

# -------------- 3. Main Regression ----------
est_main <- feols(ln_exports ~ int_post_us_treat + 
                   i(year, treat, ref = 2001)[us == 1] +   # event-study only on US
                   post:us + us:treat + post:treat | 
                   hs6 + dest^year, 
                 data = df, cluster = ~hs6)

summary(est_main)

# -------------- 4. Robustness Check ---------
# Exclude MFA products
no_mfa <- df[mfa == 0]
est_nomfa <- update(est_main, data = no_mfa)
summary(est_nomfa)

# -------------- 5. Event-study Plot ---------
es <- feols(ln_exports ~ 
            sunab(year, post * us * (treat > median(treat))) | 
            hs6 + dest^year,
            data = df, cluster = ~hs6)

iplot(es, ref.line = c(-1,0))
```

Interpretation: β̂ from `est_main` yields the semi-elasticity of exports wrt one-ppt reduction in policy-uncertainty gap.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that removing uncertainty raises expected profits, lowers option value of waiting, and encourages entry.  
• Direction: Positive. High-gap industries should exhibit faster Chinese export growth to the U.S. after 2001 than low-gap industries and than the same industries in the EU/Japan.  
• Magnitude: Prior literature on tariff reductions finds export semi-elasticities ~1–3. Because only uncertainty—not the applied rate—changed, effects should be smaller; e.g., a 10-ppt gap could raise exports by 5–10 %. I expect β ≈ 0.005–0.01 (log-points per 1 ppt).

Downstream outcomes: U.S. import prices should fall (pass-through), implying consumer welfare gains on the order of a few bps of manufacturing consumption.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (DID/DDD)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1: No differential pre-trends (parallel trends) ............... 0.8  
C2: Exogenous, predetermined treatment variable ................ 1.0  
C3: No simultaneous policies correlated with treatment .......... 0.6  
C4: Stable composition / no sorting across treatment status ..... 0.8  
C5: Correct functional form & time-varying FE suitably control .. 0.9  

Average score ≈ 0.82 → “generally credible but needs careful robustness work.”
